scenes.heading: Submitting Jobs: spark-submit & Deploy Modes
scenes.narration: Let's take a deep look at Submitting Jobs: spark-submit & Deploy Modes and how it works under the hood in Spark.

scenes.heading: What spark-submit configures
scenes.narration: The spark-submit command is the standard way to launch a Spark application on a cluster. It lets you specify the cluster manager, whether the driver runs on your client machine or inside the cluster, and how much memory and how many cores each executor and the driver receive. It also packages your application code and its dependencies for distribution.

scenes.heading: Client vs cluster deploy mode
scenes.narration: In client mode the driver process runs on the machine you submit from, which is convenient for interactive work and debugging but ties the job's life to that machine. In cluster mode the cluster manager launches the driver on a worker node, so the job keeps running even if you disconnect. Production batch jobs almost always use cluster mode for that resilience.

scenes.code:
spark-submit \
  --master yarn \
  --deploy-mode cluster \
  --num-executors 20 \
  --executor-cores 4 \
  --executor-memory 8g \
  --driver-memory 4g \
  --conf spark.sql.shuffle.partitions=400 \
  --py-files deps.zip \
  etl_job.py --date 2026-07-01
scenes.heading: A production submit command
scenes.narration: This submits to YARN in cluster mode, requesting twenty executors each with four cores and eight gigabytes of memory. The driver gets four gigabytes, and a config flag sets the shuffle partition count for the job. The py-files option ships extra Python modules to the executors, and everything after the script name becomes the application's own arguments. This single command fully describes how the job will run on the cluster.

scenes.heading: What happens after submit
scenes.narration: Once you run spark-submit, it hands your request to the cluster manager, which starts the driver in the chosen mode. The driver then asks the manager for executors matching your resource flags. The manager allocates containers on worker nodes and launches the executors, after which the driver schedules tasks onto them. From there the DAG executes as usual.

scenes.heading: Common masters
scenes.narration: The master URL tells spark-submit where to run. Passing yarn targets a Hadoop cluster, while a k8s scheme launches executors as Kubernetes pods. The local master runs everything in one JVM, which is ideal for development and unit tests but never for production scale.

scenes.text: Use cluster mode for production; size executors from your data, not habit.
scenes.narration: Match num-executors, cores, and memory to the workload and cluster capacity rather than copying a template. The right sizing avoids both idle resources and OOM failures.
